blocks.quote: A purely linear deep network, just stacked matrices with no activation function between them, has a loss surface with no spurious local minima at all. Every critical point is either a global minimum or a saddle. \citeauthor{saxe2014deep} (\citeyear{saxe2014deep}) showed this analytically for deep linear networks; \citeauthor{kawaguchi2016deep} (\citeyear{kawaguchi2016deep}) extended the result to deep nonlinear networks.
blocks.section: Non-convexity comes from the non-linearities, not from depth

blocks.quote: So where does the non-convexity of real networks come from? From the activation functions. ReLU, sigmoid, GELU: every nonlinearity bends the function and creates the possibility of bad local minima. Depth alone is harmless. This is why residual connections help so much: each residual block is asked to learn only a small adjustment to the running state, so the overall transformation stays close to linear, and the loss surface stays well-behaved. \citeauthor{lu2017expressive} (\citeyear{lu2017expressive}) reviews the broader picture.

blocks.quote: Sharp minima, flat minima, and the oldest debate in deep learning
blocks.section: Sharp minima, flat minima, and the oldest debate in deep learning

blocks.quote: The intuition is old: a minimum inside a wide, flat basin should generalize, because small perturbations of $\theta$ keep the loss low. A narrow, sharp minimum memorizes the training set but blows up on test.
blocks.section: Sharp minima, flat minima, and the oldest debate in deep learning

blocks.quote: \citetitle{keskar2016largebatch} (\citeyear{keskar2016largebatch}) sharpened this empirically: large-batch SGD finds sharper minima than small-batch SGD, and the sharp-minimum runs generalize *worse* on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST, and TIMIT. The story is not so clean once \citeauthor{dinh2017sharpness} (\citeyear{dinh2017sharpness}) is added. Because of the ReLU and BatchNorm rescaling symmetry above, every sharp minimum can be reparameterized into an equivalent flat one. "Sharp" was not a property of the minimum. It was an artifact of the parameterization. \citeauthor{smithle2018bayesian} (\citeyear{smithle2018bayesian}) reframed SGD as approximate Bayesian inference: small-batch noise is not a bug but a prior that biases the trajectory toward wide valleys.
blocks.section: Sharp minima, flat minima, and the oldest debate in deep learning

blocks.quote: The live descendants of this debate are **Sharpness-Aware Minimization** \cite{foret2021sam}, which explicitly adds a "be flat" penalty to the loss. Too flat, and the gradient signal vanishes; too sharp, and the optimizer oscillates. SAM works because the loss depends on the data and parameters; a step that is locally flat on the training set may not be flat on the test set, so SAM evaluates the loss at a small perturbation around the current point and descends from there.
blocks.section: Sharp minima, flat minima, and the oldest debate in deep learning

blocks.quote: Train two ResNets independently on CIFAR-10 from different random initializations. They land in *different* minima, with different test errors and different predictions on hard examples. Now draw a straight line between them in weight space and plot the loss along the line. \citeauthor{garipov2018mode} (\citeyear{garipov2018mode}) showed that the loss along this straight line is *high* — the two minima are separated by a barrier — but that with a small bend in the line (a "polygonal chain"), every point along the curved path has nearly training-set error. The minima are *mode-connected*: not by a straight valley, but by a low-loss curved path.

blocks.quote: The set of well-performing weights is connected. The landscape is one big basin, full of curvature ripples and small ridges but without barriers. This is also why "model ensembling", averaging several independently-trained nets, works so well: every ensemble member is somewhere along this single low-loss manifold, and their disagreements are just different local orientations.

blocks.quote: Grokking: the optimizer slowly switches basins
blocks.section: Grokking: the optimizer slowly switches basins

blocks.quote: This shows two things about the landscape. First, the same initialization sits inside the catchment of many basins, some sharp, some flat, with barriers between them. Second, weight decay (the only thing distinguishing the two basins in this experiment) is what biases the long-time trajectory toward the flat basin. The geometry is fixed; the optimizer's path through it is shaped by regularizers.
blocks.section: Grokking: the optimizer slowly switches basins

blocks.quote: The "one big valley" claim needs a caveat. Swap two neurons in any hidden layer and the network computes exactly the same function, but its position in weight space changes by a large distance. This permutation symmetry means every "true" minimum corresponds to an astronomical number of equivalent positions in raw weight space. A 50-layer net with 256 neurons per layer has roughly $(256!)^{50}$ equivalent positions for each minimum, more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. The landscape is full of copies of the same minimum, scattered across weight space like reflections in a hall of mirrors.
blocks.section: Grokking: the optimizer slowly switches basins

blocks.quote: This is why a raw straight-line interpolation between two independently trained networks is high-loss: without accounting for the copies, the line passes through garbage (random mismatches between equivalent copies), not through the low-loss valley. \citeauthor{garipov2018mode} (\citeyear{garipov2018mode}) sidestepped this by searching for a low-loss *curved* path between the two minima; aligning permutations is a later technique for testing *linear* mode connectivity. The "one connected valley" claim is true in the symmetry-reduced parameter space, where equivalent copies are identified as the same point. In raw parameter space the same statement is false; the same minimum has many disconnected copies. \citeauthor{amit1989modeling} (\citeyear{amit1989modeling}) reviews the broader symmetry structure of neural-network landscapes.
blocks.section: Grokking: the optimizer slowly switches basins

blocks.quote: SGD travels in an almost one-dimensional subspace
blocks.section: SGD travels in an almost one-dimensional subspace

blocks.quote: PCA on the iterates $\theta_0, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_T$ recovers what is actually happening. For both SGD and Adam on VGG-9, the first **two** PCA directions capture between **40% and 90%** of the variation in the descent path; the remaining directions are nearly silent. Gradient descent is effectively low-dimensional.
blocks.section: SGD travels in an almost one-dimensional subspace

blocks.quote: Putting it together
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: The picture that survives the most careful empirical work \cite{li2018losslandscape,garipov2018mode,choromanska2015loss} is roughly this:
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 1. The landscape is one connected valley. Local minima are exponentially rare. Saddles dominate but are easy to escape with stochastic noise. Independent runs find different points, all connected by low-loss paths (once permutation symmetries are factored out).
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 2. Skip connections reshape the topology. They replace chaotic multi-basin terrain with one smooth basin. As a side effect, trainable 100-layer nets exist.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 3. Width flattens. Wider networks have wider basins. Sharpness and generalization error track each other when measured with filter normalization.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 4. Optimizers are nearly one-dimensional. The trajectory lives in a subspace spanned by a handful of PCA directions; the other $10^{10}$ coordinates are nearly constant. The optimizer sees a noise-smoothed version of the surface, not the raw one, which is why small batches help \cite{mandt2017variational}.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 5. Flat generalizes, sharp memorizes, but only when "flat/sharp" is defined by a scale-invariant measure (filter-normalized Hessian, local entropy \cite{chaudhari2016entropysgd}, or SAM \cite{foret2021sam}). The naive measures are broken by ReLU rescaling.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 6. Architecture determines what basins exist. A plain feedforward net and a ResNet have different loss surfaces over the same data, because they have different reachable weight configurations. Choosing an architecture is choosing which family of basins the optimizer can land in.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: 7. The same basin can be reached by very different paths. SGD, Adam, momentum, and SAM all settle into basins of comparable quality on a given architecture; the regularizer (weight decay) and the noise (mini-batch size) decide which basin wins over long training \cite{grokking}.
blocks.section: Putting it together

blocks.quote: The energy-landscape concept in physics is much older — suggested by René Marcelin in 1913 and given its first quantitative potential-energy surface for H + H₂ by Eyring and Polanyi in 1931; \citeauthor{wales2003energy}'s \citeyear{wales2003energy} book is a modern synthesis. It was first applied to neural networks by \citeauthor{hopfield1982} (\citeyear{hopfield1982}), whose associative-memory networks literally used the energy of a physical spin system as the loss function. The systematic 2-D visualization that turned the metaphor into a diagnostic tool is \citeauthor{li2018losslandscape} (\citeyear{li2018losslandscape}); their `tomgoldstein/loss-landscape` GitHub repo is the de-facto standard for loss-landscape plots today.
blocks.section: Putting it together
